context: simplest residential form · finishing-led, minimal MEP

brief.intro: New to this project type? A standalone house is the simplest residential building type — a single detached dwelling with a straightforward structure and no shared walls, pools or bespoke finishes to complicate the programme. Once the shell is weather-tight, the schedule is almost entirely a finishing sequence: waterproofing wet areas, screeding and tiling, second-fix MEP, painting and joinery, each trade following the last through the same rooms. There is little to commission — a house has no plant room, no risers and no life-safety systems — so the real programme risk sits in material delivery (doors, sanitaryware, kitchen units) and in keeping the finishing trades moving through the house without treading on each other.

the point where the roof and envelope stop rain ingress, allowing internal finishing to start reliably.

must_get_right: Get the shell weather-tight early — internal finishing cannot start reliably until the roof and envelope are sealed.
Protect the wet-area waterproofing test — nothing downstream (tiling, second fix) should start until it's tested and released.
Sequence material orders — doors, sanitaryware, kitchen units — against the finishing programme rather than ordering everything up front; the wrong item on site too early just gets damaged or stored.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. A single, straightforward structure means the finishing sequence carries most of the activity count.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard 6-day working week; wet-area waterproofing curing and test time is held as real non-working duration rather than compressed.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structure & roof → weather-tight envelope → MEP first fix → wet-area tanking & test → tiling → second fix → snagging → handover. With no plant or shared services to coordinate, the critical path is essentially the finishing-trade sequence moving room by room.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and material selections frozen before construction start; a single continuous mobilisation; no shared-wall or multi-unit interfaces to coordinate.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: A single small site with limited laydown space; finishing-trade crews are sequenced through the same rooms one after another rather than run in parallel.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: late material delivery, a wet-area waterproofing test failure, and weather delaying roof/render works. Contingency is held before wet-area testing and before handover.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary); controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 for the field finishing sequence — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
